title: The Vase Miskina Breadline
sources: ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), siege of Sarajevo findings
ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Sarajevo siege count
ICTY Dragomir Milosevic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29/1-T), siege period
Burg & Shoup, The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1999), Chapter 5 on the siege
content:
Vase Miskina street — known since the war as Ferhadija — runs through the heart of Sarajevo's Ottoman quarter, a pedestrian thoroughfare lined with shops and cafés that connects the central market at Baščaršija to the broader civic spaces around the eternal flame and Marshal Tito street. On the morning of 27 May 1992, several dozen civilians stood in a queue along Vase Miskina waiting for bread to be distributed from a bakery that had been operating in the street. At approximately ten o'clock, three mortar rounds fell among them. The shells killed approximately twenty civilians and wounded more than a hundred others.

The siege of Sarajevo had begun in early April 1992. By the end of May the city was substantially encircled by Bosnian Serb forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, deployed on the surrounding hills and ridgelines. Artillery, mortars, and direct-fire heavy weapons were emplaced on positions overlooking the city — at Trebević to the south, on the slopes of Hum and Žuč to the north, on the heights around Lukavica and Ilidža. The encirclement was not yet complete in the operational sense — the Tunnel of Salvation under the airport runway would not be completed until the summer of 1993 — but the city was within range of indirect-fire weapons across nearly its entire urban area.

The Vase Miskina shelling occurred against this backdrop. The ICTY Galić Trial Judgment, which dealt with the period of Stanislav Galić's command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from September 1992 to August 1994, found that the corps maintained a sustained pattern of shelling and sniping of civilian areas and civilian targets in Sarajevo throughout that period. The 27 May incident preceded Galić's command and was therefore not within the temporal scope of that case, but its place in the siege's narrative — as the first widely reported single-incident massacre of civilians in the city — informed the chamber's reasoning on the campaign's character. The Karadžić chamber, addressing the siege as a whole, treated the incident among the early evidence of a pattern that the chamber found constituted a campaign of terror against the civilian population.

The attribution of the shelling has been disputed in some accounts. Bosnian Serb representatives at the time and in subsequent statements claimed that the shelling had been carried out by Bosnian government forces against their own civilians for propaganda purposes. United Nations observers in the city at the time, and subsequent ICTY findings, concluded that the rounds had been fired from positions held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The trajectory analysis available to international observers — the angle of arrival of the rounds, the location of likely firing positions consistent with that angle — supported the attribution to Bosnian Serb forces. Burg and Shoup, in their account of the siege, treated the Bosnian Serb counter-claim as one of a recurring pattern of attribution disputes that arose around individual incidents during the siege and that were generally resolved by international observers in favour of Bosnian Serb responsibility.

The political significance of the Vase Miskina shelling exceeded its immediate human cost. The incident occurred on the day before a scheduled European Community foreign ministers' meeting in Lisbon, and the news of the shelling produced an immediate decision to impose sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. United Nations Security Council Resolution 757, adopted three days after the shelling on 30 May 1992, established a comprehensive trade embargo on the FRY. The resolution did not end the war, did not loosen the siege, and did not alter the operational situation in Sarajevo. It marked, however, the international community's first concrete policy response to the conduct of the siege, and one that would constrain Belgrade's freedom of action for the remainder of the conflict.

The street itself, renamed Ferhadija after the war, remains a pedestrian thoroughfare. A small plaque in the pavement marks the spot where the shells fell, one of the modest commemorations that Sarajevo has chosen for the dozens of similar incidents that the siege produced across forty-four months.
